# Hostname verdicts both language implementations must agree on.
#
# The companion to urlguard-addresses.txt, and it exists because that file
# covers addresses only. Host normalization drifted between the two
# implementations precisely where nothing compared them: Python's rstrip
# removed every trailing dot where Go's TrimSuffix removed one, and Python
# compared a raw Unicode string against a rule the resolver then evaluated on
# an IDNA-folded name. Both suites read this file and must produce the same
# verdict for every line.
#
# Format: <host> <allow|block> <why>

# -- ordinary public names -------------------------------------------------
example.com             allow  ordinary public name
docs.example.com        allow  ordinary public name
EXAMPLE.COM             allow  case is normalized, not meaningful
example.com.            allow  one trailing dot is a rooted name, still public

# A suffix must match a label boundary, not a substring. local.dev is an
# ordinary public zone and has nothing to do with .local.
docs.local.dev          allow  .local is not a suffix of this name
internal.example.com    allow  'internal' as a label, not the .internal zone
mylocal                 allow  no dot, not the .local zone

# -- local-only name spaces ------------------------------------------------
localhost               block  the loopback name itself
app.localhost           block  the .localhost zone
printer.local           block  mDNS
wiki.internal           block  the .internal zone
nas.home.arpa           block  RFC 8375 home network zone
PRINTER.LOCAL           block  case must not evade the rule

# -- trailing dots ---------------------------------------------------------
# A rooted name is the same name. Go trimmed one dot and Python trimmed all,
# so these three disagreed between the two processes.
localhost.              block  rooted loopback name
printer.local.          block  rooted mDNS name
printer.local..         block  two trailing dots is still the same name
wiki.internal..         block  two trailing dots is still the same name

# -- non-ASCII -------------------------------------------------------------
# Refused outright rather than normalized. getaddrinfo treats U+3002, U+FF0E
# and U+FF61 as label separators and NFKC-folds fullwidth letters, so each of
# these resolves as its ASCII spelling while reading as something else. Go's
# resolver folds none of it. An internationalized name must arrive as
# punycode, which is ASCII and which both resolvers use on the wire anyway.
wiki．internal           block  U+FF0E fullwidth stop folds to wiki.internal
printer．local           block  U+FF0E fullwidth stop folds to printer.local
nas．home．arpa           block  U+FF0E fullwidth stop folds to nas.home.arpa
wiki。internal           block  U+3002 ideographic stop folds to wiki.internal
wiki｡internal           block  U+FF61 halfwidth stop folds to wiki.internal
ｌｏｃａｌｈｏｓｔ               block  fullwidth letters NFKC-fold to localhost
éxample.com             block  non-ASCII; supply the punycode form instead

# Punycode is ASCII and is what the wire carries, so it is accepted and the
# suffix rule reads the real labels.
xn--80ak6aa92e.com      allow  punycode for a public internationalized name
xn--p1ai.internal       block  punycode label under the .internal zone
